questions.q: What does burning the boats mean in Higgins's metaphor?
a: Removing retreat so you must commit to Plan A
Preparing a fallback before you begin
Quitting a stable job to travel the world
Cutting ties with people who doubt you
questions.why: The overview explains that a general destroyed his own boats to eliminate retreat, leaving only one option.

questions.q: According to Higgins, what does merely considering a Plan B do?
a: It lowers the odds that Plan A will succeed
It makes Plan A easier to achieve
It keeps your options open and safe
It sharpens your decision-making
questions.why: The overview quotes Higgins saying that contemplating a backup sets off a loop that makes the main plan less likely.

questions.q: What bold move did Higgins make at sixteen?
a: He left high school and entered college two years early
He started his first investment firm
He became New York's youngest press secretary
He joined the Miami Dolphins front office
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes him dropping out, passing the GED and starting college early to earn more money sooner.

questions.q: What does Higgins suggest you do with anxiety before a big moment?
a: Accept it and work with it instead of denying it
Suppress it and focus only on the task
Wait for it to pass before taking action
Avoid the situation until you feel calm
questions.why: Lesson 2 says denying anxiety backfires; Higgins turned his own nerves into excitement through positive self-talk.

questions.q: Which principle does Higgins offer for taking on new adventures?
a: Big leaps over incremental gains
Slow and steady improvement
Always keep a fallback option
Learn mainly from your failures
questions.why: Lesson 3 lists big leaps over incremental gains, urging readers to think bigger rather than settle for small steps.
